name: Grand Teton National Park
blurb: Sagebrush flats, willow wetlands and the elk, moose and wolves of Jackson Hole.

tip.title: Remove the wolves
tip.text: Wolves came back to the park from Yellowstone. Set Gray wolf to -100% and watch elk and moose, then the willow and aspen they browse.

notes: The story and why it matters come from the Wikipedia articles listed below (Grand Teton National Park, Elk, Moose). Individual species and links have not been checked one by one. Feeding links that match a GloBI (Global Biotic Interactions) record are marked in the node details, with a link to the records. A few links were added from GloBI records.

nodes.desc: Deep winter snow drives elk, moose and pronghorn down from the high country to the valley floor, and its spring melt feeds the Snake River.
Burns renew conifer forest and aspen stands. Park agencies now use fire management plans after earlier suppression reduced plant diversity.
Nutrients in valley and sagebrush soils that plants draw on, replenished by decomposers.
The shrub of the sagebrush flats, the most widespread habitat in the park and home to about 100 grass and wildflower species.
Shrubs along the river and wetlands such as Willow Flats, and a main winter and summer browse for moose.

nodes.name: Quaking aspen
nodes.desc: A leafy tree of the valley slopes and river terraces, eaten by elk, moose and beaver.
Migrates between summer range in Yellowstone and the surrounding forests and winter range on the National Elk Refuge, passing through the park. Eats mostly sedges, forbs and tree sprouts in summer.
Browses willow and eats aquatic plants, and stays near waterways and wetlands in the park.
Eats a wide mix of forbs, shrubs and grasses on the open sagebrush flats. Prey for coyotes, wolves and bears.
A browser of shrubs and wildflowers, recorded eating fireweed and thimbleberry.
A large grazer of the valley meadows and sagebrush flats.
Cuts aspen and willow along the river and builds dams that create ponds and wetlands.
Hunts ground squirrels and young hoofed animals and scavenges carcasses.
Scavenges carcasses, including wolf kills, and eats insects and small prey.
Takes waterbirds and small mammals and scavenges carrion along the river.

nodes.name: American black bear
nodes.desc: Omnivore that eats plants, insects and young animals, and scavenges carcasses.
Returned to the park from Yellowstone after being wiped out in the early 1900s. Preys on elk and moose, with moose calves and weak animals most at risk.

nodes.name: Grizzly bear
nodes.desc: Eats army cutworm moths, roots, berries, pine seeds and carcasses, and takes elk calves.
Break down dead plants, animals and dung, returning nutrients to the soil.

story: Grand Teton National Park in Wyoming covers about 310,000 acres, including the 40-mile Teton Range and the northern part of Jackson Hole. Over 1,000 vascular plant species, 300 bird species and more than a dozen fish species live here. Some rocks are nearly 2.7 billion years old.
matters: It is 10 miles south of Yellowstone, and together with surrounding national forests they form the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem, one of the largest intact temperate ecosystems.
